analysis.one_liner: Blocks all US greenhouse gas rules until China, India, and Russia adopt similar ones.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor and died in committee when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar every federal agency from issuing or enforcing any regulation that reduces carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gas emissions until three officials certify in writing that China, India, and Russia have proposed, implemented, and enforced substantially similar reductions [S2][S3]. It would go further and void every such US regulation already in effect until that certification is made [S2][S3]. In practice, that would wipe out the EPA's existing climate rules, such as limits on power plant emissions, indefinitely. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil, and gas producers and any power plant or factory facing emissions limits would benefit if the bill passed, because all federal greenhouse rules would be nullified indefinitely [S2][S3]. The waiting condition is written so it likely never clears: it requires certification that three foreign governments both adopted and enforced measures matching the EPA's proposed US reductions [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA or any federal agency from implementing or enforcing any regulation, proposal, or action that reduces carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gas emissions until the EPA Administrator, the Energy Information Administration head, and the Commerce Secretary certify in writing that China, India, and Russia have proposed, implemented, and enforced substantially similar reductions [S2][S3].
Nullifies any existing US regulation, proposal, or action requiring greenhouse gas emission reductions — rules already in effect before the bill passed — until that certification is made [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, ordinary people would bear the health and climate costs of unchecked emissions — more air pollution from power plants and no federal limits on the emissions driving warming — while foreign emissions limits had no bearing on US pollution levels [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would void regulations already in effect, removing limits on power plant and industrial emissions and leaving the United States with no federal greenhouse gas rules regardless of what other countries do [S2][S3].

The foreign-action trigger gives China, India, and Russia effective veto power over US air quality rules, and the certification could be withheld indefinitely, making the prohibition functionally permanent [S3].

US emissions cuts would be delayed on the theory that other countries must act first, even though US pollution affects US public health directly; supporters cite the Senate's 1997 Byrd-Hagel resolution against treaties binding developed countries without matching developing-country commitments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers no public benefit in exchange for removing all federal greenhouse gas limits, including rules already in force. Its stated rationale — that major foreign emitters should act too — is a negotiating position, but the mechanism is not a negotiating tool: it is a flat prohibition on any US rule until a certification that depends on other countries' actions. For anyone who values federal limits on air pollution and climate emissions, the cost is total and the benefit is nil.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Energy and Power Subcommittee three days later, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. John Fleming (R-LA) introduced the bill on November 17, 2015, and no member joined as a cosponsor [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S5].
On November 20, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where it stayed for the remainder of the 114th Congress, which ended January 3, 2017, with no further action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position or spent anything to kill it; the bill died of inattention. The public is better off that existing greenhouse gas rules were never nullified, and fossil fuel interests are better off only in the sense that no momentum was built for either direction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no rules were voided

for.name: John Fleming
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors joined from either party, no committee action was taken, and no votes were recorded, so the partisan shape beyond the sponsor's party is not in the record [S1][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would nullify every federal greenhouse gas rule in effect and bar new ones indefinitely, removing the main federal constraint on fossil fuel emissions [S2][S3]. Ordinary people would bear the resulting air pollution and climate costs [S2][S3].

Rules limiting power plant emissions, including those already in force, would have no force or effect until foreign certification, sparing coal-dependent generators compliance costs while the public absorbs the pollution [S3].
